subject: mathematics
question_text: Prove by mathematical induction that 1³ + 2³ + 3³ + … + n³ = n²(n + 1)²/4.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.25, chapter 4 MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION, Short Answer question 1(i). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The split gives one mark to each of the four moves an induction proof is marked on — the base case, the hypothesis, the inductive step and the closing appeal to the principle — and leaves the opening statement step unmarked, matching every other card in this chapter. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, and Mathematical Induction supplies one of them on almost every paper. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. LINES EXPANDED 2026-09-14 (founder direction, modelled on the Maths-2A and Maths-2B expansions): every move is written on its own line, with the reason or the arithmetic shown before it is used; the steps, marks and split are unchanged.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — the nth term, the five moves, and what you add to both sides in the third step.
formula_note: The closed form here, n²(n+1)²/4, is the standard sum of cubes — easy to confuse with the sum of squares, n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, proved elsewhere in this unit: cubes square the bracket [n(n+1)/2]² with no (2n+1) factor; squares keep the (2n+1) factor with no square on n(n+1). A sibling card also sums cubes, of multiples of 4, scaled by 16.

steps.label: Write the statement
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks, but never skip it — the nth term and the full S(n) line are what Step 3 works on.

recall.must_convey: That the nth term is n³ and S(n) is the full statement, the sum of cubes up to n³ equals n²(n+1)²/4.
accept: the nth term is n cubed and s of n says the sum of cubes equals n squared into n plus one squared over four
general term n cubed then write out s of n in full
each term is a cube so the nth term is n cubed
nth term n cubed ani rasi s of n rastam

steps.why: The series is given as a pattern. Naming the nth term as n³ turns three sample terms into an expression you can add to both sides later.
common_mistakes: Writing the nth term as n² and proving the wrong identity.
Leaving S(n) unwritten, so Step 3 has no line to work from.
steps.memory_tip: The nth term is n³. The right side is the square of the sum formula: n(n+1)/2 squared is n²(n+1)²/4.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. Work out BOTH sides separately at n = 1 and say they are equal.
lines: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 the left side is 1 and the right side is 1 times 4 over 4, which is also 1, so S(1) is true.
accept: left side is one cubed which is one and right side is four over four which is one
put n equals one in both sides and both come to one
the first case gives one on each side
n equals one pettina rendu sides one vasthai

steps.why: Induction needs a true first case to start from. However good the inductive step is, without S(1) there is no proved case for it to work from.
common_mistakes: Asserting S(1) is true without working out both sides.
steps.memory_tip: At n = 1: left side 1, right side 4/4 = 1. Write both, then write that they are equal.
lines_compact: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume it for ONE value k and number the line (1) — Step 3 quotes that number.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

lines.text: (take S(k) as true for one natural number k)

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is assumed true for some k in N — the sum of cubes up to k³ equals k²(k+1)²/4 — and the line is numbered (1).
accept: assume it for k so the sum up to k cubed equals k squared into k plus one squared over four
suppose s of k holds and call that equation one
take it as true for one value k in the naturals and number the line
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one ga rastam
reject: let it be true for k
then I assume s of k

steps.why: This is the assumption the method uses. It is taken as true for one value only, and Step 3 has to show that it then holds for the next value.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for ALL k, which assumes what is being proved.
Not numbering the line, so Step 3 cannot cite it.
steps.memory_tip: Assume for one k and number the line (1). Step 3 adds the next term to that numbered line.
lines_compact: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. Add (k+1)³ to both sides of (1), then take (k+1)² out as a common factor.
lines: So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

recall.must_convey: That (k+1)³ is added to both sides of (1), (k+1)² comes out as a common factor, and k² + 4k + 4 factorises to (k+2)², giving the formula with n replaced by k+1.
accept: add k plus one cubed to both sides then take k plus one squared out and the bracket becomes k plus two squared
put in the next term take the common factor out and you get k plus one squared into k plus two squared over four
k squared plus four k plus four is a perfect square so it becomes k plus two squared
next term add chesi common factor teeste k plus two squared vasthundi
reject: I show s of k plus one

steps.why: The added term (k+1)³ shares the factor (k+1)² with the assumed sum. Taking that factor out leaves k² + 4k + 4, which is (k+2)² — exactly the bracket the formula needs at k+1.
common_mistakes: Adding (k+1)² instead of (k+1)³ as the next term.
Expanding everything into a quartic instead of factorising, which takes longer and is easy to get wrong.
Stopping before writing = R.H.S, so the step does not show what was asked.
steps.memory_tip: Add (k+1)³, take (k+1)² out as a common factor, and k² + 4k + 4 = (k+2)².
lines_compact: So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. One sentence, one full mark.

lines.text: (S(1) is true, and S(k) true gives S(k + 1) true,
so S(2), S(3), … are true in turn)

lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That S(1) is true and S(k) implies S(k+1), so by the principle of mathematical induction the result holds for every natural number n.
accept: since s of one is true and s of k gives s of k plus one by the principle of mathematical induction it holds for all n
hence by p m i the statement is true for every natural number
the base case and the inductive step together give it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni natural numbers ki true

steps.why: The earlier steps prove two single statements — one about n = 1 and one about a step. Only the principle turns them into a claim about every n.
common_mistakes: Writing only 'hence proved' and never naming the principle.
Claiming it for all real numbers instead of all n ∈ N.
steps.memory_tip: The closing sentence names the principle and is worth a full mark on its own.
lines_compact: Hence, by the principle of finite
